We were motes of dust to them, insignificant in the passage of time. The stars - communicating on their own medium still largely inaccessible to us, the'sea' as they called it - had debated the significance of humans ever since we'd left our atmosphere. The lines between the animate and the inanimate had been blurred. Stars saw all things as living, in some sense - some more so than others, of course. Stars did not quite propagate, or survive. They simply..... were, until they weren't. And they thought for that entire time. To the stars, it turns out, they'd just assumed we were intelligent. They assumed all things were intelligent. Perhaps not capable of communication or comprehension, but still possibly thinking on some plane of existence. "They are, therefore they think." It was a compelling point of view, all things considered. If we could talk to stars, why not to other things? Aquinas sighed, as he shifted in his chair to get back up. Only a moment's rest. The basic politics has been discussed, the nature of stars, what they wanted and did not want..... it had been largely business. There'd been moments of insight and true talk, here and there, but for the most part it was the simple procedure of extraterrestrial contact the System's scientists had sorted out centuries before. Stars were independent bodies, but didn't much care about anything else - they felt no pain, and did not care what installations we built around them, or how we traversed them. The only thing they requested was that they be allowed to think, as long as possible. Aquinas rose from his chair, and crossed the room. The auxiliary controls in his room had been another nice touch. Built for emergencies, but..... it's not like what he was about to do could hurt. He reached down, fiddled with some controls - that transmitted very complicated directions to a very big machine on the ship - and was linked into the communication medium, a swirling ball of plasma that was magnetically controlled to produce new shapes, configurations, and energy patterns. After a moment in silence, standing over the controls, bowed with his hands flat against the surface of the countertop, he spoke up. "Logla, you listening?" He asked. The star had no name. No stars did. It had agreed on one, however, given the nature of human communication. So it had been decided to name it Logla, and the star agreed that when we said Logla, it would answer. And it did. "I'm here, Aquinas." He piqued up at this, as he always did. It recognized him, despite the communication medium - and the fact he hadn't said much of note. There was some other means of identification..... which was surprising, given stars had no need for such identification. A quick learner, it seemed. "What thoughts do we have to attend to?" Aquinas chuckled. Stars did little else but think, so Logla had an issue phrasing any activity as something other than thinking. It understood the activities, well enough, but it just preferred not to speak of them in human terms. "Nothing to attend to, today, Logla. I just wanted to think together." A soft humming came from the speaker. This indicated the star was processing, preparing to vocalize thoughts. A very human mannerism. Eventually, Logla spoke up. "This sounds agreeable. It is something stars do often, and enjoy." "Enjoy? You don't talk about emotion a lot, Logla. To be honest..." Aquinas pondered whether to continue, but shrugged and went on anyway. "We weren't quite sure you felt things like we did. You know, felt them as much." The star hummed again. "Most likely not, Aquinas. But we still feel. Feeling is just another form of thinking, after all." Aquinas smiled. "That's one way of putting it," Aquinas sat back down in his chair, no longer nervous about how poorly unsupervised contact might go. Logla was a very nice star, so far. It was pretty damn unlikely he'd upset it. He wasn't even sure what could. At this thought, Aquinas sat, tapped his chin, then pressed the button to continue speaking. "What makes you feel, Logla? And what do you feel?" The star hummed, for a long time. At least a minute. This was unusual - most thoughts took stars very little time, because they had very, very big brains. Finally, the star continued, "Everything makes me feel, Aquinas. How could it not? Stars have a long time to think..... and with a long time, everything becomes worth thinking about," The star hummed shortly, then continued, "I feel..... happy. Sad. Curious." Aquinas raised an eyebrow. "Not afraid? Not angry?" "Those are unintelligible to me. Rethink your thoughts for me, Aquinas?" This was a fun oddity of inter-species communication. Stars rarely did not understand each other, they had learned - it was only external interference that caused issues with communication. Logla did not quite understand the idea of'untranslatable' concepts yet - but it very well understood interference, and just acted like it was that. "Well, anger..... it's..... when something is wrong. Or when something endangers you. Do you ever feel so strongly, you want to..." Aquinas realized that there wasn't really much the star could do, or want to do. Stars could not move. They could not act. They could barely even perceive, it turned out. They largely existed just to think. Anger would be meaningless for them..... they couldn't act out. And fear..... they couldn't retreat. Aquinas paused, and shook his head. "I'm sorry, Logla. I don't think there's a way to rethink that thought without interference." A soft humming, then Logla replied, "That's okay, Aquinas. I understand, though I am curious and sad." "Sad?" Aquinas rested his face on his arm, holding his button down with the other hand. "Why, Logla?" "I wish I could understand. Curiosity that goes without answer..... it causes sadness. A wish things were different," Logla spoke slowly, far more slowly than normal. "Curiosity answered brings happiness." "That's all?" Aquinas asked, quietly. "You feel happiness and sadness only then?" "No..... We feel happiness to know. We enjoy thinking. And some things are pleasing to think about. While others..... we feel sadness to confront. And some things are sad to think about," Logla's speech was very slow now. "Some things are both." "I understand. We feel similarly. We call it'bittersweet'. I have no idea if that thought will be conveyed right, but..... it's a pairing of opposites. Like dark and light, at once." Stars understood light very well. "It seems contradictory, but..." "But it isn't. I understand. The thought conveyed poorly, but I think the thought too. There are many experiences that bring both happiness and sadness. Like you." Aquinas nodded, quietly. The gesture would be translated by the machine, but he still reaffirmed it, and said, "Yes. Like you too." "Aquinas, we - I - are happy to know you exist. That you think like we do. And that we can speak. There have been so few..... so few that can speak to us, besides us," The star said, and Aquinas nodded. The stars had mentioned other people that spoke to stars. They hadn't said much about them, but it was much more than mankind had expected to hear. We'd assumed stars were the only non-Earth intelligence. "We love thinking new thoughts. We love the curiosity it brings to know something we can't think is there. But we feel sad about it..... to know that we can't think it, ever. And we feel sad when they leave." "Leave?" Aquinas asked, his own curiosity now burning. "Leave. Stars..... we think a long time. Even as we die, we think. A star's light goes out long before their thinking does. Their thinking slows, their part in the sea fades, but they are there. We are there. We have watched many like you leave us..... and you leave us so quickly. So suddenly..." The star hummed, and this time, the note was different, a rich and deep tone. Aquinas listened to the star's song, for a few seconds, but it stopped abruptly as the song continued. "We wish you could be with us for longer. That you could think like us. But to do so would mean you do not think as yourselves..... and that is what we love to hear about..." The star hummed again, and this time, the countertop thrummed as it resonated with the note. Aquinas' bones sang along with the note. "To think about your time, compared to our time..... that is the greatest thought of sadness we stars have." Aquinas wiped away a tear from his face. The immensity of a star's life..... it was unthinkable, how many peoples it must have watched go extinct, and yearned to hear from, one more time. "Us too, Logla. We both wish for more time." "All who think do," Logla said, then hummed quietly, while Aquinas sat, and listened to its song.

But if it hits a much heavier steel ball, it will be deflected, and with it most of its energy. Shock waves behave in a very similar manner: A shock wave in air hitting a human will be reflected almost entirely, whereas a shock wave in water is able to pass right through a human, simply because water is very similar in density and elasticity to tissue.," "Water doesn't compress, so doesn't absorb the energy like air does. article: Parameterized algorithms are a very useful tool for dealing with NP-hard problems on graphs. Yet, to properly utilize parameterized algorithms it is necessary to choose the right parameter based on the problem at hand. The choice of parameter can significantly impact the complexity and running time of the algorithm. One common approach is to use structural parameters, which capture some aspect of the structure of the input graph. Examples of structural parameters include treewidth, vertex cover, and feedback vertex set. These parameters can often be computed efficiently and can be used to construct algorithms that have a polynomial dependency on the parameter. Another approach is to use problem-specific parameters. These parameters are chosen based on the specific problem and its inherent characteristics. Might as well last as long as I can. The path is blocked behind me, so I move forward. There's no way to see what's ahead of me. I sit down and wait for it, and about twenty minutes later a little tray flies down on a parachute. I unbuckle the clips, and inside sits a finger-sized piece of jerky and a little 8-oz thermos. Didn't think it was actually going to bring me what I asked for. I look up to where the rover climbed the wall, and I see it sitting there, a smiley face on it's little black ball. article: Yes, exactly like that. A bit longer answer: ohm's law is more intuitive, V IR. In a batteryoutlet, you have a voltage differential that will push electrons through the wire and create a current. Ohm's law helps to explain the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance in a circuit. Voltage, measured in volts (V), is the electrical potential difference between two points in a circuit. This difference creates a driving force for electrons to flow through the circuit. Current, measured in amperes (A), is the rate at which electric charge flows through a circuit. The current is directly proportional to the voltage and inversely proportional to the resistance. Resistance, measured in ohms , refers to the degree to which a material opposes the flow of electric current. It is an electrical property of a material that determines how much current flows through it for a given voltage. Ohm's law states that the current flowing through a conductor in a circuit is directly proportional to the voltage applied across it and inversely proportional to the resistance of the conductor. Thus, the equation V IR is used to express Ohm's law, where V is the voltage, I is the current, and R is the resistance. In summary, Ohm's law is an important fundamental principle in understanding basic electrical circuits, and it helps to explain the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance. It is a useful tool for designing, analyzing, and troubleshooting electronic circuits.

article: In this paper we address the problem of unsupervised gaze correction in the wild, presenting a solution that works without the need for precise annotations of the gaze angle and facial features. Our approach uses a generative adversarial network (GAN) to learn a mapping from input images with arbitrary gaze angles to output images with corrected gaze angles. The GAN is trained by minimizing a combination of the adversarial loss and a perceptual loss, which measures the difference between the generated and target images in terms of their high-level features. To achieve this, we first preprocess the input images by detecting the face and estimating the gaze angle using a pre-trained face and gaze estimator. We then pass the preprocessed images through our GAN to produce the corrected gaze images. Finally, we post-process the output images by blending them with the original input images to preserve some of the original appearance. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach can successfully correct gaze in a wide range of unconstrained environments, and outperforms several state-of-the-art methods on the publicly available MPIIGaze dataset.

article: A number of applications (e.g., AI bot tournaments, sports, peer grading, crowdsourcing) use pairwise comparison data and the Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model to evaluate a given collection of items (e.g., bots, teams, students, search results). Past work has shown that under the BTL model, the widely-used maximum-likelihood estimator (MLE) is minimax-optimal in estimating the item parameters, in terms of the mean squared error. However, another important desideratum for designing estimators is fairness. In this work, we consider fairness modeled by the notion of bias in statistics. We show that the MLE incurs a suboptimal rate in terms of bias. We then propose a simple modification to the MLE, which "stretches" the bounding box of the maximum-likelihood optimizer by a small constant factor from the underlying ground truth domain. We show that this simple modification leads to an improved rate in bias, while maintaining minimax-optimality in the mean squared error. In this manner, our proposed class of estimators provably improves fairness represented by bias without loss in accuracy.

article: Cross domain image matching between image collections from different source and target domains is challenging in times of deep learning due to i) limited variation of image conditions in a training set, ii) lack of paired-image labels during training, iii) the existing of outliers that makes image matching domains not fully overlap. To this end, we propose an end-to-end architecture that can match cross domain images without labels in the target domain and handle non-overlapping domains by outlier detection. We leverage domain adaptation and triplet constraints for training a network capable of learning domain invariant and identity distinguishable representations, and iteratively detecting the outliers with an entropy loss and our proposed weighted MK-MMD. Extensive experimental evidence on Office dataset and our proposed datasets Shape, Pitts-CycleGAN shows that the proposed approach yields state-of-the-art cross domain image matching and outlier detection performance on different benchmarks. The code will be made publicly available.

article: This will probably get buried as I'm late to the party, but couldn't resist - the prompt is too good! This isn't that horrifying either, I just came up with it in traffic and kind of went with it. Good practice I guess. Bank station. The busiest on the network, nearly a hundred thousand passengers each morning travel through here, arriving to make their daily trudge through the city of London to their jobs. Most of them work in banking. They're easy to spot, with suits from Saville Row, shirts from Jermyn Street, and morals darker than the deepest recesses of Soho. Profiling a target is a doddle, and the execution comes naturally. Growing up on the estate, I was never going to be allowed into the rarefied air of the Bank of England or Lloyds of London. Once Mum had her benefits cut, I had to pay my way, it's not uncommon. Lads on BMX bikes move weed and whatever else they can get their hands on, but I was never tough enough to look after myself in those gangs. I ended up shoplifting, a quick stroll over to Oxford Circus, snip off the tags and tailgate a tourist out. Easy. Too easy. There's no skill to shoplifting, not like pickpocketing. I had a good teacher, a modern day Fagin if you will, though the flat caps of Oliver Twist were replaced by snapbacks, tags still attached of course. After a few years I went solo, still staying in touch with my old mates to make I wasn't stepping on anyone's toes. You rarely get a nicely worded letter from these boys if you're on their patch. Bank is so busy I can act with impunity, plenty of bankers for everyone. This one was perfect. I saw him run through the barriers, flustered, late, fumbling with his oyster card. He carefully checked his wallet before throwing the card in there, a flash of blue still visible as he slid it into his inside jacket pocket. This was almost too easy. I moved towards the door where he was stood, ostensibly to pick up a discarded copy of the Metro from a seatback. I didn't feel like reading, but it looks natural, and a freesheet is a bloody good prop, even if it is plastered in the latest story of debauched footballers. He was lost in his own world, checking his phone every five seconds, looking for the red blinking LED that has enslaved so many in this city. Even easier. He goes for the door, I watch his shoulders, tailing him through the barriers as he taps the wallet on the reader. He's going left, towards the exit for the Bank. I feint left and go right, my shoulder crashing into his chest. A flutter of newsprint and a thousand tuts from the commuters and I'm home and dry, the soft leather wallet nestling in my jacket now. I cross the platforms and jump on a tube heading east, time for a spot of lunch and a bit more work. Westfield Stratford, a hell of a shopping centre, and close enough to home to know shorten my commute back. I'm in need of a new t-shirt and I guess old habits die hard. Maybe a quick lift to top up the beer kitty for tonight. Quick scan and boom. A yank, can spot them from a mile off. They always dress like they're going into battle, rucksacks, sunnies, hat, bottles of water, as if anywhere outside of the USofA lacks even basic amenities. Not that I'm complaining, all those pockets make theft a doddle. I stroll past to get a look at the bag, but before I can she turns, and I freeze. "Hey, can you help me?" I was right, definitely American. Right, new tack. The accent goes on, no more wide boy charm, time for the full Cumberbatch.'I certainly hope so my dear, how can I be of service to you?' She smiles sweetly, and asks for some advice. Don't hang around with reprobates like me would be a good start, luv. Keep it moving "Let's walk and talk, it's a big place and we won't see it all from standing still." I introduce her to a few shops, she's in London for 2 days before her friends fly in. "Well it's a terrible shame for a lovely lady like you to be all alone. I wouldn't be much of a gentleman if I didn't offer to keep you company for a while. Fancy a spot of lunch?" She's in. Wahaca. Chelada. Tostada. We chat, it beats eating lunch alone. She's tidy, decent chassis on her in a pair of shorts and a hollister tee. Long blonde hair and a tendency to use'like' as punctuation, I'd guessed she was from California long before she divulged that fact. Whether it was the light glinting off her straw coloured locks, or the refraction of it through the amber beer, I felt good. I pay for lunch and take my leave, demanding only a hug as payment for her company. As we embrace I slide fifty quid out of her unguarded pocket, which covers lunch and my time. Off home, stopping on the way to pick up a henry and some king size rizla for the evening ahead. Through the door, trainers off and jacket over the chair, time for a brew. Fucking hell, I almost forgot, that wallet I took this morning. Chatting to that American bird distracted me more than I thought. Good job I wrote my number on the back of a tube ticket for her. I try not to bring evidence home if I can help it. Wallets get stripped of the good stuff and binned, phones are fenced down the local before I get home, the more unusual stuff I take a view on. Let's take a look at the wallet. It's nicer than I thought. Hand stitched, the leather is softer than I've ever felt before. The tip of the oyster card still peeks out from it. Two hundred bats cash. Nice. American Express Platinum, standard, and a nice way to assuage my guilt. Anyone with one of these can afford to lose a few bob. Few more bits and bobs. Mostly crap. Still, no stone unturned and all that. There's a slip of paper tucked inside, folded carefully. It's a photo. Who even carries photos any more? A photo of a baby in an incubator. Shit. That's what he was looking at. On the phone. He wasn't waiting for notification, he was looking at the wallpaper, the very same photo. Fuck it, he's got a digital copy of it then, nothing fifty pence at Boots can't solve for a reprint. There's more paper on the other side of the pocket, but it doesn't look like cash, I take a quick look so I can bin what I don't need on the way to the pub. Order of Service. Oh Christ. She was called Molly. He buried her yesterday. Poor Bastard. His driving licence is still in the wallet. I have to send this back. It's not fair. This is never what I set out to do. The address goes on the envelope, I'll throw it in the post box tomorrow somewhere in the city. Not popping evidence in the box at the bottom of the tower. For now, let's work on this henry. - I'm at Oxford Circus today, I don't want to go back to Bank in case I see him again. I'm not afraid, just ashamed. The letter goes in the postbox, swallowing at least some of my guilt in its wide red mouth as well. Time to go to work. Same routine, I take a seat and wait for some idiot tourist to advertise themselves. Another yank dressed like they're off to battle Rommel jumps on, and I grab my prop. No footballer today though. Seems some banker decided to take the quickest route from the top of the walkie talkie to the slabs below. I've seen that name before. Not half an hour ago as I dropped it through the slot.

article: We consider the age-old problem of allocating items among different agents in a way that is efficient and fair. Two papers, by Dolev et al. and Ghodsi et al., have proposed interesting solutions to this problem. Dolev et al. present a protocol called "Fair Division without Envy" that ensures each agent receives a fair share of the items without any agent envying another. Their protocol uses a cryptographic approach and requires a trusted central authority to generate and distribute cryptographic keys that are used by the agents to select items. Ghodsi et al., on the other hand, propose a decentralized solution to the problem using a blockchain-based protocol called "FairSwap." Their protocol allows agents to exchange items among themselves fairly and without any intermediary or central authority. The fairness of the protocol is ensured through the use of smart contracts that enforce the rules of the exchange. Both of these papers present innovative solutions to the problem of fair allocation of items among agents, with different trade-offs and assumptions. It is worth noting that the practicality and efficiency of these protocols still need further investigation and experimentation, but they open up new avenues for future research in this area.

article: I'm feeling adventurous, with a few hours before I'm due to meet my estate agent, I decide to take a walk around what could be my new neighbourhood. It's a cheap part of town, full of dark, five or six storey buildings lining narrow alleys, each one seems to be caged in iron, a few have twisted metal balconies overlooking the dirty streets below. I can hear cars speeding down the main road behind me, some parts of the neighbourhood are pretty popular, or so I'm told. I figure I'll see a lot of them when I'm living here. I walk further away from the noise. A single car rumbles past me. Mercedes. Nice. I continue walking. I start to feel completely alone, I notice that my surroundings are devoid of the sounds of everyday life, there is no furniture on any of the balconies either. A door to my right is cracked open. I look inside. The place is empty and a thin layer of dust covers everything. I decide I'll go up to the balcony if I can, to get a better look at the city. When I reach the second floor something catches my eye, a dark figure is leaning over the rusted rails..... Oh, he's going to jump! I've always been fast. I rush out and grab is waist, flinging him with all my strength back indoors. A briefcase goes skidding across the floorboards. The guy is skinny, but strong. He pushes himself away from me and scowls. "You'll thank me later" I say smiling. The look he gave me was as if I'd told him to go jump again. He scowls again and tells me to stay back. He pulls a gun from his coat pocket. "How many others?" He demands of me. "Uh..." I have no idea what to say. Is this guy a nut? In the distance comes the sound of rumbling, another car. "Shit" he says, scanning the floor, gun held tight between white knuckles. "What's up?" I say. He tells me to shut the fuck up. A man appears in the doorway, then slumps forward clutching his belly. "Oh god" he says, looking at his gun as if it could save him. "He was too early" he tells me, eyes wide with fear. The man in the doorway remains silent, lying in a puddle of blood. I vaguely become aware of a ringing in my ears. The skinny guy points at the red rose in the dead man's hand. He runs, forgetting the briefcase and me. Shaken, I get up and peek out to the balcony, by now the car is pretty close. It's the same silver Mercedes, but it's coming in the opposite direction. I know enough to guess that this was some sort of hand off. Fear starts squeezing my shoulders and stiffening my joints. I know enough to guess this scene won't look good. Then I do something that is probably the stupidest thing and best I could do at this point. I take the briefcase. I know it probably has money in it, who says no to that? I still have a few seconds. I climb up more steps to the roof. The buildings are all joined here. I run along the roofs with my heart banging against my chest. Finally I reach the end of the street, I climb down fire escape, trying to ignore the yelling men behind me. A taxi, what luck. I offer a silent prayer and hop in. "Ridgeway please." The men are still a few rooftops behind, they wouldn't have seen me get in. A few days later and I'm reclining on my brand new couch, in my brand new apartment, in the nice part of town. This approach helps to minimise Gibbs phenomena by limiting the influence of oscillations from one subinterval to the neighbouring ones. The Pad'e-Chebyshev type approximation has been widely used in approximating functions with highly oscillatory behaviour, such as singular functions and functions with discontinuities. However, when a Pad'e-Chebyshev type approximation is applied to a piecewise smooth function, Gibbs phenomena may occur at the borders of the subintervals. Gibbs phenomena are the overshoot and undershoot of the approximation at the borders of subintervals, caused by the abrupt change in the function's behaviour at these points. To overcome this issue, the PiPCT algorithm applies the Pad'e-Chebyshev type approximation separately to each subinterval, limiting the influence of neighbouring subintervals, which helps to reduce the overshoot and undershoot near the borders of the subintervals. The proposed PiPCT algorithm provides high accuracy in approximating piecewise smooth functions by reducing the oscillations and removing the Gibbs phenomena, while at the same time maintaining the computational efficiency of the Pad'e-Chebyshev type approximations. The algorithm has been tested on several examples and has shown to be efficient in approximating piecewise smooth functions accurately. article: The classical perceptron is a simple neural network that performs a binary classification by a linear mapping between static inputs and outputs and application of a threshold. For small inputs, neural networks in a stationary state also perform an effectively linear input-output transformation, but of an entire time series. Choosing the temporal mean of the time series as the feature for classification, the linear transformation of the network with subsequent thresholding is equivalent to the classical perceptron. Here we show that choosing covariances of time series as the feature for classification maps the neural network to what we call a 'covariance perceptron'; a mapping between covariances that is bilinear in terms of weights. By extending Gardner's theory of connections to this bilinear problem, using a replica symmetric mean-field theory, we compute the pattern and information capacities of the covariance perceptron in the infinite-size limit. Closed-form expressions reveal superior pattern capacity in the binary classification task compared to the classical perceptron in the case of a high-dimensional input and low-dimensional output. For less convergent networks, the mean perceptron classifies a larger number of stimuli. However, since covariances span a much larger input and output space than means, the amount of stored information in the covariance perceptron exceeds the classical counterpart. For strongly convergent connectivity it is superior by a factor equal to the number of input neurons. Theoretical calculations are validated numerically for finite size systems using a gradient-based optimization of a soft-margin, as well as numerical solvers for the NP hard quadratically constrained quadratic programming problem, to which training can be mapped.

article: Mobile-edge computing (MEC) has recently emerged as a cost-effective paradigm to enhance the computing capability of hardware-constrained wireless devices (WDs). In particular, we consider task dependency between the two WDs, where the input of a task at one WD requires the final task output at the other WD. Under the considered task-dependency model, we study the optimal task offloading policy and resource allocation (e.g., on offloading transmit power and local CPU frequencies) that minimize the weighted sum of the WDs' energy consumption and task execution time. The problem is challenging due to the combinatorial nature of the offloading decisions among all tasks and the strong coupling with resource allocation. To tackle this problem, we first assume that the offloading decisions are given and derive the closed-form expressions of the optimal offloading transmit power and local CPU frequencies. Then, an efficient bi-section search method is proposed to obtain the optimal solutions. Furthermore, we prove that the optimal offloading decisions follow an one-climb policy, based on which a reduced-complexity Gibbs Sampling algorithm is proposed to obtain the optimal offloading decisions. We then extend the investigation to a general multi-user scenario, where the input of a task at one WD requires the final task outputs from multiple other WDs. article: The fuzzy K -means problem is a generalization of the classical K -means problem to soft clusterings, i.e. clusterings where each points belongs to each cluster to some degree. Although the classical K-means problem assigns each point to a single cluster, the fuzzy K-means problem assigns each point to all clusters with degrees of membership representing how likely the point belongs to each cluster. The fuzzy K-means problem is also known as FCM (fuzzy c-means) and is commonly used in pattern recognition and image segmentation. In fuzzy K-means, the objective is to minimize the sum of squared distances between each point and its cluster center, weighted by the degree of membership. The degree of membership of each point to each cluster is computed using a membership function which gives a value between 0 and 1, representing the probability or degree of belief that the point belongs to that cluster. The membership function is updated iteratively until convergence is reached. Fuzzy K-means has several advantages over classical K-means, including the ability to handle overlapping clusters and the ability to assign points to multiple clusters simultaneously. It also allows for more nuanced representations of cluster membership and a finer-grained analysis of data. However, fuzzy K-means can be computationally intensive and requires careful tuning of parameters.

I smiled, trying to remain unthreatening. They had power now, but money rules the world. "Dear woman, what are you doing?" I jumped, taken aback at those words. The man, the wizened old farmer, spoke in English. Perfect English. "I'm sorry, I didn't..." "Oh," the other chimed in, a smile greeting his lips as he gathered the money strewn on the floor. "Oh she's AMERICAN. One of those. Makes sense lads." "Let's take her to get freshened up. She'll want to meet the other journos who thought they'd sneak in to'hell' to get their story!" The men laughed playfully, and pity hung over their faces as they saw my hands start to tremble. We walked along a dirt track, my muscles aching from the battle to stay afloat in the brutal sea. I had to know. Needed to know. "You understand English." It wasn't a question. I tried to ensure my voice remained strong, but it wobbled. I coughed and sea water spilled from my mouth searing my throat. The man who'd been first to reveal his English accent spoke again, handing me a freshly pressed handkerchief. "Yes dear. We do. It's taught in all our schools. We learn from a young age how to articulate and enunciate in our mother tongue, as well as an array of other languages. Mandarin, Tagalog, French..." Schools? I stopped walking. "You, you go to school?" "Well, not by your standards, which are on a par with Amazonian tribes I'd say!" The men all laughed. Their scathing tones burned my ears, and a mixture of rage and fear bubbled in me. "Our schools are more like your rich countrymen's offerings. They are private. We go to school, learn languages, maths, the sciences, art... everything and anything you could wish to turn your hand to." The second farmer held my elbow as we carried on walking the path. "You see, he said, gently, "We love our country, and our Dear Leader." "How can you love that man? That murderer! He walks around like a god on earth while his people - you! - starve!" Standing in front of the men, blocking their path, I saw their faces change. Insulting their god-king would be what killed me. "HIM?" The third man spoke, before they all broke out laughing. "Oh isn't it wonderful doing this?" the first farmer said to his friends. "That god-king, as you so incorrectly call him, is our ruse. He's what takes your attention. He's our trickster, and you are our mark." I shook my head. "No," I said. "No. The reports, from your people who escape your camps. You fear him." As we reached the end of the gravel path, the men remained silent. The stones turned to asphalt, and sitting obscured by leafy green trees was a brand new car. Not a cart powered by wood or a collection of ramshackle bikes. A car. Shiny and clean. The men stopped. Two entered the sedan. The first man leaned up against it as he stretched his arms above his head, resting them folded on his chest. "Your nation, all nations of the world. They are dirty." He shuffled on his feet, getting more comfortable. "Imagine your friend and you both have a prized vase each. It had taken centuries to create, and was now yours." I looked at him, as tears graced his eyes. "Your friend. He's not clever. He doesn't appreciate it's value. He let's everyone see it, touch it. His friends don't see the value, so they crack it. Before long the porcelain is stained, the vase is damaged and it can never be what it was. It can be fixed, but the cracks will always be its weakness. That, that is the world and every land in it." I heard the trill of a mobile phone, and one of the men in the car answered, speaking Korean. "So we're all broken?" I asked. "Yes. The wars and violence, your lack of care for the weak and elderly. The orphans abandoned by your state and the widows forced out of homes. You weaken your people from birth, brainwashing them into believing material goods are success." I snorted. "So this is paradise, right?" "The vase. After seeing what your friend did to it, you decide to keeps yours safe. So when the same friends say they want to play with it, you say it's already broken. They will pester you, and laugh at you for being weak. But they will leave it alone. "Our scientists have cured diseases your people know nothing about. Our students learn skills to ensure they are entertained without the need for your internet. Our old and infirm are housed in complexes to rival palaces! "If we told the world we could cure cancer with a simple injection, you would take, and your leaders would destroy it. Because you place value on money. Your tourists would destroy our land, our people would be forced out of their homes for hotels. We place value on our people." I stood there rigidly, not wanting to believe those words. He opened the door to the car and I took a seat. We drove through towns and villages, passing houses as beautiful as Spanish villas and French chateaux. I spoke up. "All we believe. The poverty and oppression..." "We place value on our people. When tourists visit, they are shown what we want them to be shown. We have a fool parade around with your celebrities. We turn our nation's lights off at night to avoid being seen. The escapees volunteer to leave, knowing they will never see their families again. Knowing they will eventually die alone, as so many of your elderly have done." He looked glassy eyed into the distance. "They are the true casualties of this game." We arrived at a camp, nothing like what I had come to imagine I'd find. "Your people will be told you are dead. Your family can only come here if we stage a kidnapping. article: They are similar to look at and touch, and they are made up of the same basic pieces - processor, RAM, screen, etc. However, there is a significant design difference between Android and Apples IOS. Android has been designed to be open and to run on anything - anyone can take the source code to Android and modify it to work on their specific hardware. Therefore if you design a phone with a different processer, a different type of memory, a different WiFi connection, etc - then you can simply re-write Androids code to support your gadget. Therefore, in theory, if someone has the time - you could actually re-write Android to be installable onto an Apple device. Not only is this theoretically possible, but it has actually been done URL0 IOS on the other hand is closed. Apple write it specifically for their devicies. As such, the only people who can edit the IOS operating system are Apple themselves. Therefore if you make a new device with a new processer and different RAM etc, then the only people who can make IOS work on it are Apple...... therefore Apple are the only ones who can make new IOS devicies. Each approach has its pros and cons. Android is generally much more flexible, but it can be (debatably!) argued that because IOS is written for a very small specific hardware configurations, it can be better tested and made to be more stable and is easier (again, deatable!) for developers to develop for because its a guaranteed hardware platform whereas Android could be running on just about anything.

article: Despite excellent theoretical support, Differential Privacy (DP) can still be a challenge to implement in practice. In part, this challenge is due to the very real concerns associated with converting arbitrary or infinite-precision theoretical mechanisms to the often messy realities of floating point or fixed-precision. Beginning with the troubling result of Mironov demonstrating the security issues of using floating point for implementing the Laplace mechanism, there have been many reasonable concerns raised on the vulnerabilities of real-world implementations of DP. In this work, we examine the practicalities of implementing the exponential mechanism of McSherry and Talwar. We demonstrate that naive or malicious implementations can result in catastrophic privacy failures. To address these problems, we show that the mechanism can be implemented exactly for a rich set of values of the privacy parameter and utility functions with limited practical overhead in running time and minimal code complexity. How do we achieve this result? We employ a simple trick of switching from base e to base 2 , allowing us to perform precise base 2 arithmetic. A short, precise expression is always available for , and the only approximation error we incur is the conversion of the base-2 privacy parameter back to base e for reporting purposes. The core base 2 arithmetic of the mechanism can be simply and efficiently implemented using open-source high precision floating point libraries. Furthermore, the exact nature of the implementation lends itself to simple monitoring of correctness and proofs of privacy.

article: Inferring missing facts in temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) is a fundamental and challenging task. Additionally, prior work does not explicitly address the temporal sparsity and variability of entity distributions in TKGs. article: In human-in-the-loop machine learning, the user provides information beyond that in the training data. Many algorithms and user interfaces have been designed to optimize and facilitate this human-machine interaction; however, there are still challenges and limitations to this approach. Additionally, there may be biases or inconsistencies in the user inputs, which can also affect the model's accuracy. Another challenge is the potential for human error or bias in the feedback provided to the machine learning algorithm. This can occur if the user has their own subjective understanding of the expected outcome or if they unintentionally provide misleading feedback. Lastly, the process of human-in-the-loop machine learning can be time consuming and costly, as it typically requires significant resources and human effort. This may not be feasible for all projects or organizations. Overall, while human-in-the-loop machine learning can be a powerful tool, it is important to carefully consider these challenges and drawbacks so that they can be mitigated or addressed as needed.

This renders its application challenging in few-shot learning scenarios, where many related tasks need to be learned, each with limited amounts of data and compute time. Thus, few-shot learning is typically done with a fixed neural architecture. To improve upon this, we propose MetaNAS , the first method which fully integrates NAS with gradient-based meta-learning. MetaNAS optimizes a meta-architecture along with the meta-weights during meta-training. During meta-testing, architectures can be adapted to a novel task with a few steps of the task optimizer, that is: task adaptation becomes computationally cheap and requires only little data per task. Moreover, MetaNAS is agnostic in that it can be used with arbitrary model-agnostic meta-learning algorithms and arbitrary gradient-based NAS methods. Empirical results on standard few-shot classification benchmarks show that MetaNAS with a combination of DARTS and REPTILE yields state-of-the-art results.

article: This wasn't how it was supposed to happen, thought Tony, as he tore down the trail. This wasn't how it was supposed to happen at all! Even conversations had taken forever, like Brendan was stressing over every word. The underbrush kept pressing in, threatening to drown him in a sea of green. We were going to hang out! Go to that boardwalk, eat junk food: just enjoy the day, not even bothering with video games! Brendan had never said how he was sick, but Tony knew that he had issues with travel. Even when he'd suggested making the trip himself, Brendan protested. Yet Tony wasn't anything if not persistent, finally making Brendan agree to a visit. Tony had been looking forward to it too: he'd never seen the coast before, and Brendan caved once Tony claimed meeting his gaming partner was just a perk for a long awaited vacation. Brendan was going to meet Tony at the airport, but instead it was..... her. Those backwards-thinking bastards! How could they?! Tony broke through the foliage, finding himself on a hill facing the sea. He couldn't remember running that far, nor expecting this view from the path he'd been taking. Before he could take in the sight, his sudden sprinting caught up to him; spying a nearby bench, he staggered towards it. " Tony, wait! " a voice called out. Her voice. " Go away! " he shouted back. She had been waiting near the baggage claim, holding a sign with one of his gamertags written on it. Tony knew that they'd PM'd each other's info before proposing the trip, so he'd thought Brendan was just pranking him. It would go along with Brendan keeping silent the last couple of days leading up to the trip. She'd said her name was Emily, and that she was Brendan's sister. Tony hadn't been able to get much more out of her while she drove, just that she was sorry Brendan couldn't make it. She'd promised to explain things better once they arrived, so Tony enjoyed the ride, keeping the conversation superficial. It wasn't until they reached the house that she delivered the news. " Tony, I'm truly sorry, but Brendan passed away three days ago. We only just heard you were coming when we checked his accounts this morning. " " Oh, really? Shoot, I really wanted to hang out right away, " Tony had said. " It'll take, what, another two before he'd back to normal? I hope I'm not imposing by staying here in the meantime. " Emily had sighed, " No no, it's..... Brendan's dead, Tony. He's not coming back. " " What are you talking about? Of course he is. " " No..... I'm explaining this wrong, it's- " Tony had stepped out of the car, shouting, " Brendan, as jokes'go, you've done better! Where you hiding, man? " Emily had followed, " He's..... he's in here. " And she led him to Brendan. " Tony, just let me explain! " Emily cried. " How could you? " he snarled back. " How could you kill him like that?! He could've come back if you didn't have those stupid traditions! Who even follows those anyways? Especially for someone our age! He was my friend, damn it! How could you take him!?! " Tony sobbed, letting his rant peter out. " How could you take him..... " The two stood there, only letting their crying break the silence. The sun dipped closer towards the horizon as they wore themselves out. Eventually, Emily walked over to the bench sat down. " Did you know, " she began, " that that revival process isn't a hard reset? Just a short rewinding of the clock? " She didn't glance over, though she seemed to be waiting for Tony. He grunted some affirmation as he lowered himself down on the other side. " There's all sorts of preconditions and what have you, but most times doctors say you get a year back every time you go through it. You've got to live that year though, before it really works again. For most people, that's enough. " When she looked over, Tony saw the sheer grief in her eyes. " But Brendan..... Brendan had ALS. " Tony just stared, not processing why that mattered. Emily continued, " What it does..... it's just cruel. That a disease could make you a prisoner in your own body..... it's just wrong. " She wasn't crying anymore, although Tony guessed that she'd cried it all out over this. " Brendan used games as an escape: for a place where he could still do all those things that were robbed of him. " For the first time, she smiled, " And that's where he met you. " " You became his reason to keep fighting it, to keep holding out hope. He always wanted to keep playing with you; as he lost more control, we modified the controls so he could keep up. He lived for those hours with you, " Emily sighed, nursing that melancholy memory to life, only to let it float away. " But we couldn't do that to him. We couldn't thrust him back into that pain, even for a moment with you. We couldn't do it. I'm sorry. " Tony didn't know what to say: what anger revulsion remained had been smothered by the truth. All that remained was a near hollowness. Not bad, really, he thought, just rather calm. He didn't know how to feel about this anymore. So he thought about Brendan. He thought about his corny jokes stupid gamertags. He thought about all the co-op matches they'd won by the skin of their teeth. He thought about all the matches they hadn't. He thought about the weirdly deep conversations they'd had waiting for screens to load opponents to join. He thought about his friend, letting the thoughts fill the void. Tony was barely aware of Emily, going through the same motions he was. And they sat there, emptily-full, as they let the sun set for them.

article: We study gains from trade in multi-dimensional two-sided markets. Specifically, we focus on a setting with n heterogeneous items, where each item is owned by a different seller i , and there is a constrained-additive buyer with feasibility constraint F . Multi-dimensional settings in one-sided markets, e.g. where a seller owns multiple heterogeneous items but also is the mechanism designer, are well-understood. In addition, single-dimensional settings in two-sided markets, e.g. where a buyer and seller each seek or own a single item, are also well-understood. Multi-dimensional two-sided markets, however, encapsulate the major challenges of both lines of work: optimizing the sale of heterogeneous items, ensuring incentive-compatibility among both sides of the market, and enforcing budget balance. We present, to the best of our knowledge, the first worst-case approximation guarantee for gains from trade in a multi-dimensional two-sided market. Our first result provides an O (log ( 1 r -approximation to the first-best gains from trade for a broad class of downward-closed feasibility constraints (such as matroid, matching, knapsack, or the intersection of these). Here r is the minimum probability over all items that a buyer's value for the item exceeds the seller's cost. Our second result removes the dependence on r and provides an unconditional O (log n) -approximation to the second-best gains from trade. We extend both results for a general constrained-additive buyer, losing another O (log n) -factor en-route. The first result is achieved using a fixed posted price mechanism , and the analysis involves a novel application of the prophet inequality or a new concentration result. Our second result follows from a stitching lemma that allows us to upper bound the second-best gains from trade by the first-best gains from trade from the "likely to trade" items (items with trade probability at least 1 n) and the optimal profit from selling the "unlikely to trade" items. We can obtain an O (log n) -approximation to the first term by invoking our O (log ( 1 r -approximation on the "likely to trade" items. We introduce a generalization of the fixed posted price mechanism - seller adjusted posted price - to obtain an O (log n) -approximation to the optimal profit for the "unlikely to trade" items. Unlike fixed posted price mechanisms, not all seller adjusted posted price mechanisms are incentive-compatible and budget balanced. We develop a new argument based on "allocation coupling" to show the seller adjusted posted price mechanism used in our approximation is indeed budget balanced and incentive-compatible.

article: It's like an airplane, but moving forward instead of up. The point of sail comes from where the wind is coming from, and how you set the sail in order to create the speed of the boat. If you want to go to a certain point, there's a direct line between the point where you are and your destination called the rum line. You can usually not go directly on that line, unless the wind is pointing in that direction. So instead, you tack through the wind (or jibe, if the wind is at your back) to use the sail to power the boat as fast as possible. It creates a zig zag line usually. I truly recommend getting out on a boat and learning a bit. article: Training multi-agent systems (MAS) to achieve realistic equilibria gives us a useful tool to understand and model real-world systems. One popular approach to training MAS is using reinforcement learning (RL), in which agents learn to maximize their own rewards based on their observations and actions. This approach is effective for simple games with a small number of agents and a limited action space, but it becomes challenging when there are many agents and the action space is large. Another approach is to use game theory, which provides a mathematical framework for analyzing strategic interactions between agents. In this approach, agents learn to play the game by predicting the behavior of other agents and finding a Nash equilibrium. This method is more robust and can handle more complex games with larger numbers of agents and more diverse action spaces. However, both of these approaches have limitations, and researchers continue to work on developing more sophisticated methods for training MAS that can handle even more complex scenarios. article: Tres Morte; a city for the unforgotten. It's wide cobblestone streets zigzagged through the city like lace. Dark gothic buildings were fitted snuggly where the roads ended. The urban sprawl's labryinthean nature and the lack of any sunlight made navigating the city difficult. Tall oil lamps dotted the paths, though they provided very little illumination. Jade hummed to herself as she pushed a steamer trunk up one of the city's gentle slopes. Foot traffic was low, as it usually was, the dead weren't in a rush to go anywhere, but occasionally she did stop and wave'hello' to a fellow pedestrian. A broad-shouldered man with a plumed hat and a blue petticoat, an old oriental hunched over his walking stick and clothed in vibrant reds and yellows; the occasional red-faced drunkard trying to convince himself that there was still something beating inside of his chest cavity. Very few of them returned her greeting. She did not allow their sullen faces to dampen her mood. She never thought of death as a loss, she thought of it simply as a transition. Of course, she was aware that the city was a poor place to live (if she could still use that word), with it's dreary decor and the lack of sunlight. But, what where the alternatives? Restless souls had tried to venture outside of it's boundaries in the past into the cracked, dry wastes beyond, with torches and improvised weapons in hand. It never amounted to much. Sometimes they would return, disappointed and maybe missing a few men. Other times they wouldn't return at all, swallowed by the darkness. The Authorities had prohibited expeditions outside of the city when the latter became more likely than the former. The cumbersome steamer trunk rolled onwards on a trolley that might've been blue once. Now it was only partially blue. The streets were filled with the sound of it's rubber wheels skidding on the uneven cobblestone. Jade was afraid that she might lose control or that the heavy leather belts strapping the trunk down might come undone. Fortunately, she made it without any unnecessary incidents. Her apartment was on the top floor of the Heffler building, which was four stories tall. The climb wouldn't have been much of a problem on it's own, however it seemed impossible for Jade's petite size. Nonetheless she released her hold on the trolley and stepped up to open the front door. It opened on its own, before Jade could reach the doorknob. "Uh, hello." said the young man standing in the door frame. He seemed to be a new arrival. You could always tell the newbies from the longtime dwellers. The smell of the city hadn't stuck to you yet. Jade blushed. He had a soft boyish face, but it was handsome nonetheless. "Hi," she replied, still a bit embarassed that he caught her unaware. The lad introduced himself as Wyatt and was, as predicted, a newcomer to Tres Morte. Jade told him that she had been here only two years herself. The truth was that she had been in the city for much longer, but if you start telling people that then they became much more prone to questions. "God," Wyatt said between gasps for breath, "How many more stairs?" "Just a few more! " , Jade giggled, standing ahead of Wyatt, just in case he dropped the steamer trunk. The gesture was cute, but Wyatt's thin, lanky frame didn't seem up to the task of climbing all those stairs lugging such weight. "If you need help, you could always ask!" "What do you keep in this? Bricks? " , asked Wyatt as the trunk bumped against another step. Just as they were nearing the top, the handle on the steamer trunk broke and it fell down the stairs. The lid broke on the previous landing and a man stumbled out. He ran down the stairs, mumbling through a dirty rag. Before Wyatt could react, Jade slid a dagger into the back of his throat. Blood soaked his shirt and soon dribbled onto the floor. Jade felt her heart flutter. She knew he wouldn't die. Nobody died in this place, but they could still feel. Jade knew that Wyatt felt every inch of that cold steel through his flesh and it made her quiver with joy. Wyatt gurgled something that might've been a scream. Jade cleaned the blade on Wyatt's shirt before sliding the slim, almost dainty little dagger into it's sheath under her petticoat. She didn't care that one of her toys ran from her. She had found something even better, though the wriggly little mouse would be likely to alert the Authorities to her location. She smiled. It would be a chase then. She was not new to evading the police, and Tres Mortes had so many nooks and crannies where she could hide.

article: I picked seven superpowers, they are applied in order of clicking. At an old age, Stan was on the verge of becoming an old arthritis-laden loony, and although popular among comic book fans, his death was comically thought to have happened twelve years ago. He wasn't as concerned with his Marvel career, and he was about ready to just move on with life, retire somewhere in the Bahamas, and just forget his comic book creations. In fact, today Stan got out of bed in his Hotel penthouse in Atlanta, to become aware of the aroma of his daily breakfast in bed. Being old did have perks, but he silently swore to himself as it was apparent the hotel staff had not thought enough to leave it within an arm's distance. Had he been like Magneto, it'd have been simple enough to pick up the stainless steel tray and place it on his lap. In fact, he could almost feel the heat of the tray on his legs, even though he often thought his senses were failing he was aware of a sudden weigh on his legs. He looked down, and - there it was - breakfast on the side table was now breakfast in bed. Amnesia was a scary thing, forgetting what just happened ten seconds ago, oh well. Worse things to forget than the struggle of getting out of bed in the morning. Stan breakfasted, arose, and summoned the bellboy to help him dress. There was a knock on the door two seconds later. "Awfully quick today, aren't you?" Stan commented in lieu of any chitchat from the bellb- hotel receptionist? While he was hoping he'd get to check out faster, he hadn't thought she'd come all the way here. Stan was aghast, "Wait, what? Sorry my dear, I was asking for the bellboy, my apologies if I disturbed you." "Where am I? Oh no, please, no. Don't tell anyone about this, I'll lose my job. I promise I'll never drink on the job again." She said as she started running awkwardly in her high heels towards the elevator. Ever confused now, Stan dressed himself, and determined this particular hotel chain wasn't worth staying in again, and promptly made his way to the airport for his twelve hour flight to the convention in which he was expected to appear. Waking in the airport, he realized it'd been a long time since he'd seen a Marvel convention. He was suddenly stifled by the need for some sunshine, and he rose to take a walk. He moved through the parking lot at an agonizingly slow pace, but he enjoyed the slower pace of his life. He was suddenly struck by an agonizingly bad smell, and had a strange proclivity to find its source. He regretted it instantly, as the first car window he looked in revealed a dead puppy, heatstroke no doubt. It made him so angry, how dare people leave their pets unattended? In fact, he was pretty sure it'd been left in there awhile, as there was freshly laid feces on the seat. He pictured the obscene comic book resolution, which would be fore the protagonist to reanimate the puppy then rip the door of the car to have the newly reborn creature jump into his arms. There was a loud bang, the airbags in the car went off as the door flew the opposite direction. The puppy jumped into Stan's arms and started aggressively licking his face. Confused, he made his way back to the airport, and walked through airport security to claim his baggage. The cranky gate guard pulled him aside for a body cavity inspection. She was about to ask him to remove his trousers when there was a loud explosion, then nothing. Stan woke up among rubble, confused, disoriented, and surrounded by medical staff. It was dark, early in the morning? Had he been out for a full day? He asked for a hand up, and was surprised when no help came. "Bro, you're fine. There are more pressing issues right now," responded a nearby cop. In his old age, Stan was used to being omitted from view by young people, but it did seem a little absurd. Until he tried to stand, that is. He sprang up with a vigor he hadn't experienced in years, so fast he had to throw his arms out to catch his balance. The arthritis, it was pretty good this morning. No joint creaks, or..... any creaks at all? Stan then saw what he had assumed were his arms, but belonged to the man behind him. Except, nobody was around him! Those were his arms! And his legs, he'd never seen massive calves like that on any man but the Hulk. He instantly looked around at the medical staff, looking for some explanation. They were all busy with injured bystanders, and Stan used the opportunity to find solitude to control his emotions. Will continue later, the three powers so far (if I haven't described them well enough) are Molecular Teleportation, Reanimation, and Muscle Manipulation. article: Sparse representation of images under certain transform domain has been playing a fundamental role in image restoration tasks. One such representative method is the widely used wavelet tight frame. Instead of adopting fixed filters to sparsely model any input image, a data-driven tight frame was proposed and shown to be very efficient for image denoising very recently. However, in this method the number of framelet filters used for constructing a tight frame is the same as the length of filters. In fact, through further investigation it is found that part of these filters are unnecessary and even harmful to the recovery effect due to the influence of noise. Therefore, an improved data-driven sparse representation systems constructed with much less number of filters are proposed. Numerical results on denoising experiments demonstrate that the proposed algorithm overall outperforms the original tight frame construction scheme on both the recovery quality and computational time.
